problem: Source states a general claim ("at all times education enables men"); candidate turns it into a past-tense "has always helped", softening the force.
replacement: At all times education enables men to defend their independence, and this is especially true in democratic ages. When all men are alike, it is easy to establish a single, all-powerful government, and instinct alone is enough to do it. But under the same conditions, men need a great deal of intelligence, knowledge, and skill to organize and sustain secondary powers. They need the same qualities to create, amid the citizens’ independence and individual weakness, free associations that are able to resist tyranny without destroying public order.

problem: Hedge/force: source says an amazing difference "cannot fail speedily to arise"; candidate says it "soon opens up".
replacement: So among democratic nations the concentration of power and the subjection of individuals will grow in proportion to their ignorance as well as to their equality. It is true that in ages of imperfect civilization a government is often as short of the knowledge needed to impose despotism on a people as the people are short of the knowledge needed to throw it off. But the effect is not the same on both sides. However rude a democratic people may be, the central power that rules it is never entirely without cultivation. It readily draws to its own use whatever little cultivation the country has, and if necessary it can look for help elsewhere. So in a nation that is ignorant as well as democratic, a striking difference cannot fail to open up soon between the intellectual capacity of the ruler and that of each of his subjects. That completes the easy concentration of all power in his hands. The administrative function of the state keeps expanding, because the state alone is competent to administer the country’s affairs. Aristocratic nations, however unenlightened, never present the same spectacle, because among them instruction is spread almost equally between the monarch and the leading members of the community.

problem: Added framing sentence ("Two things are happening at once.") and term drift: "welfare" rendered as "comfort" and then "well-being" in the same note.
replacement: [Footnote c: On the one hand the taste for worldly well-being is perpetually increasing, and on the other the government gets more and more complete possession of the sources of that well-being. So men are following two separate roads to servitude. Their taste for their own well-being keeps them from taking part in government, and their love of that well-being makes them ever more dependent on those who govern.]

problem: "stupendous tyranny" (enormous) rendered "monstrous tyranny", adding moral coloring Tocqueville did not give.
replacement: These two conditions of a nation have sometimes existed together. The last generation in France showed how a people could build an enormous tyranny within the community at the very time they were thwarting the authority of the nobility and defying the power of all kings. They taught the world at once how to win freedom and how to lose it. In our day men see established powers falling apart on every side. They see all ancient authority gasping its last and all ancient barriers tottering toward their fall, and the judgment of the wisest is troubled by the sight. They attend only to the astonishing revolution taking place before their eyes, and they imagine that mankind is about to fall into perpetual anarchy. If they looked to the final consequences of this revolution, their fears might perhaps take a different shape. For my part, I confess that I put no trust in the spirit of freedom that seems to animate my contemporaries. I can see well enough that the nations of this age are turbulent, but I do not clearly see that they are liberal. And I fear that, when the disturbances that rock the foundations of thrones have ended, the domination of sovereigns may prove more powerful than it ever was before.
